prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

That dusty bubble gum, once ubiquitous as starlings, is no more, my love. Whistling dinosaurs now populate only animation studios, the furious actions of angels causing their breasts to flop out in mannerist frescos flake away as sleet holds us in its teeth. And the bus-station's old urinals go under the grindstone and the youthful spelunkers graduate into the wrinkle-causing sun. The sea seemingly a constant to the naked eye is one long goodbye, perpetually the tide recedes, beaches dotted with debris. Unto each is given a finite number of addresses, ditties to dart the heart to its moments of sorrow and swoon. The sword's hilt glints, the daffodils bow down, all is temporary as a perfect haircut, a kitten in the lap, yet sitting here with you, my darling, waiting for a tuna melt and side of slaw seems all eternity I'll ever need and all eternity needs of me.

outputs.L3:
# On the Nature of Impermanence

There was a time when bubble gum seemed as permanent a fixture of the world as the starlings that filled the evening sky in great, swirling murmurations. Both were so common, so utterly ubiquitous, that their presence felt like a kind of law—unquestionable, eternal, woven into the fabric of ordinary life. And yet both have vanished, quietly and almost without notice, leaving behind only the faint residue of memory. Their disappearance serves as a humbling reminder: even the things we assume will always be there, precisely because they are everywhere, are not exempt from the slow erosion of time.

This same erosion touches even our most deliberate attempts at permanence. The mannerist frescoes that once adorned chapel walls with elaborate human dramas are fading, their pigments dulled by centuries of light and damp air, their figures slowly dissolving into the plaster from which they emerged. Even humbler structures—the utilitarian bus-station urinals, function stripped of any pretense toward beauty—crumble under the weight of years, or are torn down deliberately to make way for something newer, something momentarily more relevant. Whether cherished as art or dismissed as mere infrastructure, all human constructions share the same fate: they are destined either to decay on their own or to be destroyed by our own hands in the name of progress.

Even nature, which we so often invoke as the standard of permanence against which human transience is measured, offers no true refuge from this law. The sea, which appears eternal in its vastness and constancy, is in fact never the same from one moment to the next. Its waters are always moving, always departing, always being replaced—an unceasing exchange that only appears static to those who watch from a distance too great to perceive the change. What looks like permanence is simply motion too vast and too slow for us to easily register.

Perhaps it is because of this universal impermanence that each of us is given only a finite store of experiences and memories—a limited set of addresses, so to speak, to which we can return in moments of both great joy and great sorrow. We cannot generate infinite new places within ourselves to house every feeling that arises; instead, we are asked to make do with what we have, revisiting the same handful of recollections again and again, finding in them enough sustenance to carry us through whatever comes.

And yet, within this framework of loss and limitation, something remarkable emerges. To sit with someone we love, waiting together for a meal to arrive—an moment so ordinary it barely registers as an event at all—can feel like the whole of eternity condensed into a single, quiet instant. It asks for nothing extraordinary, no monument, no lasting fresco, no permanent structure. It exists only in that moment, and yet it is enough. Perhaps this is the quiet consolation hidden within impermanence itself: that we do not need forever to touch something eternal. We only need each other, and the simple willingness to be present, for however long we are given to be present at all.
outputs.L4:
**Nothing Stays**

The bubble gum I stuck beneath the desk in third grade
is gone now—scraped away by some janitor's hand,
or fossilized in landfill, indistinguishable from dirt.
The frescoes in that chapel outside Florence
are surrendering their blues to centuries of breath,
tourists exhaling their slow erasure with every awestruck sigh.
The tide that touched my ankles this morning
has already forgotten the shape of my feet,
pulled back into the vast amnesia of the ocean.

Everything is loosening its grip.

My grandmother's hands, once quick with flour and dough,
now tremble around a teacup like something borrowed.
The photograph on the mantel yellows a little more each year,
her wedding dress fading from ivory to the color of old paper.
Even the mountains are dissolving, grain by grain,
into rivers that carry them toward seas that also will not last,
because nothing does—
not glaciers, not stars, not the particular green
of this specific summer's leaves,
not the version of myself that woke up this morning,
already someone slightly different
than the one who fell asleep.

The gum dissolves. The paint flakes. The water retreats.
The hands shake. The dress fades. The mountain erodes.
Turn and turn and turn, and everything
is in the process of becoming something else,
or becoming nothing,
or becoming absence
wearing the shape of what it used to be.

And yet—

Here we are, you and I,
standing in this kitchen that smells like garlic and rosemary,
waiting for the rice to finish,
waiting for the timer's small electric cry,
your shoulder against my shoulder,
your hand loose in mine,
not saying anything important,
not needing to.

The impermanence doesn't frighten me right now.
It doesn't have to.
Because this—
this exact moment of waiting together,
of hunger not yet fed,
of your breathing next to my breathing,
of the light doing its ordinary gold thing
across the countertop—

this is enough eternity for me.

Let the rice finish or not.
Let the timer sound or stay silent.
Let everything else dissolve into whatever it's becoming.

I have this.
I have you, waiting beside me.
And for now, for this instant that will not return
and does not need to—

this is whole.
This is complete.
This is all the forever I require.
outputs.L5:
# The Art of Whistling

There's something remarkable about whistling—that simple act of pursing one's lips and pushing air through them to create melody. It's one of the few instruments we carry with us always, requiring no strings, no reeds, no electricity. Just breath, and shape, and intention.

Think about the last time you heard someone whistling. Perhaps it was a stranger on the street, lost in their own world, marching to a tune only they could fully appreciate. Or maybe it was a parent, whistling while doing dishes, the sound drifting through the house like a thread connecting one room to another. That casual, unselfconscious whistling—performed for no audience but oneself—might be one of humanity's purest expressions of contentment.

Whistling appears across cultures and centuries. Shepherds developed whistled languages to communicate across valleys and mountains, encoding entire sentences into pitch and rhythm. Sailors whistled work songs to coordinate their labor. Children whistle to summon dogs, to signal friends, to fill silence with something playful and their own.

And yet, despite its ubiquity, whistling remains oddly private. Not everyone can do it well, and those who can often can't explain how. Ask a skilled whistler to teach you, and they'll struggle to articulate the exact position of tongue, teeth, and lips that produces that clear, bright tone. It's a skill passed through trial and error, through childhood afternoons spent blowing air uselessly until, suddenly, a note emerges.

There's also something inherently cheerful about whistling—hard to whistle while angry or despairing. That connection between the physical act and emotional state suggests our bodies know something our minds sometimes forget: that joy can be practiced, summoned through breath and rhythm, one clear note at a time.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal free-verse poem about impermanence that ends with a tender, mundane moment of love in a diner.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Hours Do When No One's Looking**

The clocks in this town have started melting sideways,
dripping into gutters where they collect like mercury,
and no one seems alarmed—
the mailman still delivers yesterday's light,
folded into envelopes marked *fragile.*

I watched a church tower fold itself into origami,
becoming a paper crane that flew off
with someone's grandmother tucked inside its wing,
her voice trailing behind her like a scarf
unraveling in the wind: *remember me, remember me,*
already fading to a hum, then to nothing,
then to the memory of a hum.

The moon keeps forgetting its own face.
Some nights it's a coin spent long ago,
other nights it's just a rumor
the sky tells itself to fall asleep.

I asked a stranger for directions
and he turned into the road itself,
stretching out beneath my feet,
whispering *this is the only way, and it is already ending.*

Even my shadow has stopped trusting me—
it leaves early these days,
slipping out from under my shoes
to go sit somewhere else, alone,
practicing its own disappearance.

The trees undress before winter
like they're shedding decades,
not seasons, and somewhere
a photograph of my childhood home
is being eaten by soft yellow light
until only the doorframe remains,
holding nothing, holding the shape of nothing.

But here—

in this diner that smells like coffee grounds
and rain on vinyl booths,
you reach across the table
and wipe a smear of ketchup
from the corner of my mouth
with your thumb,
laughing without meaning to,

and for a moment
nothing dissolves.

The neon sign outside flickers *OPEN*
into the dark like a heartbeat,
and you say *you always do this,*
and I say *I know,*
and the coffee is going cold
and neither of us moves to fix it,

because this—
this small, unspectacular thing—
this is the one hour
I don't want saved.
I just want it
lived.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poetic prose piece addressed to "my love," blending strange, decaying imagery (frescoes, urinals, dinosaurs) with a meditation on transience and eternity.
counterfactuals.output:
My love,

I want to tell you about the fresco I found peeling from a wall that no longer holds a ceiling—saints with their faces rubbed to blank ovals, gold leaf gone the color of old teeth, and still, still, some hand centuries dead had made a mouth curve like it meant something. I stood there in the rubble and the pigeon-shit and thought of you.

I want to tell you about the urinal in the bar that closed in 1987, porcelain gone the yellow of a smoker's finger, a cathedral of small failures, men's names carved into it like it was the only stone they'd ever get to mark their passing. Someone wrote *I was here* and didn't sign it. I understood him completely.

And the dinosaurs—my love, the dinosaurs—all that magnificent tonnage, all that thunder in the ribs, reduced to a smear of carbon in a shale bed some grad student will chip at with a soft brush for a soft grant, cataloguing the exact shape of a hunger a hundred million years cold. They ruled the earth the way we think we rule anything. Then they were weather. Then they were rock. Then they were oil in the veins of engines that would drive us to look at them behind glass and feel, absurdly, nostalgic.

I bring you all this decay because I don't know another way to talk about love that doesn't lie.

Everything is leaving. The fresco is leaving the wall one flake at a time. The urinal is leaving its function, becoming only an object, then not even that—someday just dust in a dumpster in a town that's also leaving, slower, the way glaciers leave, the way the moon leaves, an inch a year, patient as anything that has nowhere else to be. You are leaving too. I am leaving. We are two mouths saying *I was here* into a century that will paint over us, that will pour concrete over us, that will find our bones so anonymous they'll have to guess our hungers from the wear on our teeth.

But here is the strange mercy: the saints' faces are gone and still someone photographs the wall. The urinal is gone and still I tell you about it, and now you carry it too, this porcelain ghost, this small ugly eternity. The dinosaur is dust and fuel and myth and the terrible longing of children who were never even born yet when it walked, and still it moves something in us, still it is *here*, transfigured, refusing entirely to be over.

So love me like a fresco, love—half-erased and gaudy with old gold, love me like graffiti in a dead bar, a name with no signature, love me like a beast too big for its own extinction, so big it leaves a shadow that outlasts the sun that cast it.

We are temporary. So was the paint. So was the porcelain. So was the terrible, sunlit Cretaceous noon.

Nothing stays. And yet: everything that was ever loved becomes, in some cracked and fossil way, forever.

Stay a while anyway. Let's be ruins together.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write something in the style of a modern romantic poet—melancholic, image-heavy, full of odd juxtapositions—that concludes with two people waiting for food together.
counterfactuals.output:
**Late Reservation**

You said love was a kind of weather
and I believed you the way I believe
in the moon's stupid loyalty—
distant, borrowed light, still showing up.

We are always describing hearts
in terms of hardware: broken, open,
heavy as a toolbox left in rain.
Meanwhile the actual heart
just keeps time like a metronome
nobody asked to hear.

I think of the ex who taught me
to check the milk before I pour it
and how tenderness, too, has an expiration—
sniff first, then trust.

Grief arrives like a waiter
who's forgotten your order
but not your face.
He keeps coming back
with water you didn't ask for,
apologizing in a language
made of ice cubes.

There is a hospital-blue hour
between afternoon and evening
when everyone in the city
seems to be driving home
to someone they no longer touch.
I drove home to you.

You were reading the specials aloud
in a voice like a hymn
nobody's sung in years—
half-devotion, half-habit.
I watched your mouth make shapes
around words like *seared* and *reduction*
and thought: this is the closest thing
I have to prayer now.

Outside, the streetlamp flickered
like a faith losing its nerve.
Inside, the candle between us
performed its small tragedy—
wax weeping onto linen,
no one comforting it.

We didn't talk about the future.
We didn't talk about the past
sitting in the empty chair beside us,
uninvited, ordering nothing,
just breathing on the silverware.

Instead we waited.
The kitchen door swung open, shut,
open, shut—a lung
learning to trust the air again.
Our hands did not touch
but they hovered near each other
like two continents
before the drift.

Somewhere a pan hissed.
Somewhere something was almost ready.
And we sat there, unhurried,
unhealed, half-hopeful,
watching the door
the way you'd watch a life
you weren't sure you deserved—

just two people
at a table built for want,
waiting for the food to come,
willing, for now,
to let hunger be the only honest thing
between us.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a lyrical, stream-of-consciousness meditation on time and loss that turns into a love poem about ordinary happiness.
counterfactuals.output:
**what the hours keep**

time is a faucet left running in a house
we no longer live in—

I think of my grandmother's hands,
how they became her mother's hands,
how mine are already practicing
to be someone else's absence,

and the light does that thing
where it comes through the blinds
in stripes like a ladder
nobody climbs,

and I lost so much before I knew
losing had a name—
a dog, a decade, a version of my father
who still laughed at his own jokes,

the clock on the stove blinks 12:00
forever, unfixed, a small stubborn ghost,
and I used to think grief was a door
but it's more like weather,
it just becomes the air you're standing in—

*

but then—

you, making coffee too loud in the next room,
the spoon against the mug like a bell
for no church I know,

and I think: this.
this is the thing they didn't warn me
would also be time—

not just the leaving but the staying,
the way you leave your socks
in every doorway like a trail
back to something worth finding,

ordinary Tuesday, ordinary rain,
your hand finding mine
without even looking,
like it already knew the way,

and maybe this is the secret
nobody says loud enough—

that the same river
taking everything from you
is the one you're drinking from,
right now, this glass,
your mouth,

that happiness isn't the absence of loss
but a small fire
built anyway,
in the same wind,

and I'll take it—
the burnt toast, the bad radio station,
your laugh that startles the cat,

let the clock keep running.
let the water keep leaving.
I'm just glad
I get to be thirsty
next to you.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem that mixes nostalgic and grotesque imagery (bubble gum, frescoes, urinals) with reflections on mortality, ending on a quiet, domestic scene of contentment.
counterfactuals.output:
**Pink Eternity**

The bubble gum I chewed at seven
still hangs somewhere, pink and eternal,
stretched thin as the skin on a saint's throat
in the fresco where God's finger
almost touches Adam's, almost
grazes the gum-pink cheek of him,
that soft explosion of created light.

I think of frescoes crumbling in churches
no one visits anymore, plaster flaking
like old scalp, saints losing their faces
to damp and time and the slow
indifference of centuries—
how even divinity needs restoring,
needs some man on scaffolding
with a toothbrush and patience.

In the men's room of the train station,
urinals gleam like ivory tusks,
white as teeth in a skull, white
as the wall behind the crucifix,
and a man hums an old tune
into the porcelain silence,
his reflection ghosting in chrome,
already halfway to vapor.

We are all just passing through
some public architecture of the body—
gum losing its sweetness by the minute,
paint losing its saints,
water rushing everything
down into the pipes of forgetting.

But tonight the kitchen light is on.
My wife stirs soup that smells of thyme
and something green from the garden.
The dog sighs at my feet, twitching
toward a dream of rabbits.
Steam fogs the window
where our reflections blur together,
soft as any fresco,
and I am not thinking of urinals
or the pink ghost of my childhood mouth—

only this: her hand passing me a spoon,
the small clink of it against the bowl,
how ordinary and how entire
this moment is, how it asks
for nothing but itself,
this one warm hour
before the long dark
finds us anyway.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
